blocks.text: The Jews also relate that the דוכיפת dukiphat brought Solomon the שמיר samir, that is, a little worm by whose power the hardest stones of the temple were split. So it is found in Cholin, in the place cited above: דוכיפת שהודו כפות וזהו שהביא שמיר לבית המקדש [col. 347] Dukiphat, the bird whose crest is bound up; it is the one that brought the little worm Samir to the house of the sanctuary. Whoever can may read a long tale about this in the tractate Gittin ch. 7, fol. 68. a. b. The gist is that Solomon, on the advice of Asmodaeus, king of the demons, sent to the nest of this bird, which it keeps in the mountains among the hardest rocks; and that the chicks found there were shut up by Solomon's servants in transparent glass. Since the mother no longer had access to them, she brought the worm שמיר samir, at whose touch the glass at once burst apart and was shattered. For the samir, they say, has such power that it splits not only glass but even the hardest of all things. Therefore Moses used it to cut and engrave the gems of the Ephod, and Solomon to dress the stones of the temple without any iron tool. I have thought this worth noting because in Greek writers too the hoopoe is said to break through all obstacles, not indeed by the power of a worm, but by the force of a certain herb. Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 26: Ἔτυχε δὲ ἐν τῷ τοῦ τείχους ἐρημοτέρῳ ὅδε ὁ ὄρνις παιδοποιησάμενος, ἔν τινι ῥήγματι λίθου ὑπὸ τοῦ χρόνου διαστάντι, ἐκεῖν ὁ τοῦ τείχους μελεδωνὸς, ἰδὼν ἔνδον τὰ βρέφη, κατήλειψε τὸν χηραμὸν τῷ πηλῷ· καὶ ὑποστρέψας ὁ ἔποψ, ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν ἀποκλεισθέντα, πόαν ἐνόμιζε, καὶ προσήνεγκε τῷ πηλῷ. ὁ δὲ κατεῤῥύη, καὶ προσῆλθε πρὸς τὰ αὐτοῦ ἐκεῖνος τέκνα. εἶτα ἐπὶ νομὴν ἦξεν, αὖθις οὖν ὁ αὐτὸς ἐπήλειψεν ἄνθρωπος· καὶ ἡ ὄρνις τῇ αὐτῇ πόᾳ ἀνέῳξε τὸν χηραμὸν καὶ τὸ τρίτον ἐπράχθη τὰ αὐτά. [Etyche de en tō tou teichous erēmoterō hode ho ornis paidopoiēsamenos, en tini rhēgmati lithou hypo tou chronou diastanti, ekein ho tou teichous meledōnos, idōn endon ta brephē, katēleipse ton chēramon tō pēlō; kai hypostrepsas ho epops, hōs eiden auton apokleisthenta, poan enomize, kai prosēnenke tō pēlō. ho de katerrhyē, kai prosēlthe pros ta autou ekeinos tekna. eita epi nomēn ēxen, authis oun ho autos epēleipsen anthrōpos; kai hē ornis tē autē poa aneōxe ton chēramon kai to triton epratchthē ta auta.] When this bird had hatched its young in the most deserted part of a wall, in a crack of a stone opened by age, and the keeper of the wall, having noticed the chicks inside, had plastered over the crack with mud, the hoopoe on its return, seeing the wall blocked, brought a herb and applied it to the mud. This at once dissolved, and she went in to her chicks, and then went back out to feed. And when the same man had plastered the wall over again, the bird opened it once more with this same herb; and this happened a third time. You see in both accounts chicks shut in by human contrivance [III, 113], and the mother hoopoe opening these barriers by a hidden power in order to help them. So it is very likely that the one fable arose from the other.

To the same effect are Solomon's conversations with the hoopoe in the Sura of the Qur'an entitled The Ant; and the embassy it undertakes for Solomon to the queen of the Sabaeans; and the springs hidden deep in the earth revealed by it to Solomon. Hence the pseudo-Prophet says: لا تقتلوا الهدهد فان كان دليل سليمان علي بعد الما وقربه [lā taqtulū al-hudhud fa-inna kāna dalīl Sulaymān ʿalī buʿd al-mā wa-qurbih] Do not kill the hoopoe, for it used to show Solomon how far off or how near the waters were, that is, how far they lay below the surface of the earth. For, as Ibno Abas relates, كانت له الارض كالزجاجة يري من باطنها [kānat lahu al-arḍ ka-al-zujāja yarī min bāṭinihā] the earth was for it as transparent as glass, so that it saw to the bottom. Naphi objects: كيف يبصر الما من تحت الارض ولا يري الفخ اذا غطي له بقدر اصبع من التراب [kayfa yubṣiru al-mā min taḥt al-arḍ wa-lā yarī al-fakhkh idhā ghuṭṭiya lahu bi-qadr iṣbaʿ min al-turāb] How does it see the waters that are under the earth, and not see a snare when it is covered with dust a finger's breadth deep? And Ibno Abas replies: اذا نزل القضا عمي البصر [idhā nazala al-qaḍā ʿamiya al-baṣar] When the decree (of God) descends (that is, when God so wills), its sight is blinded. Thus, just as the Hebrews do with the bird dukiphath, so the Arabs insert many trifles about the hoopoe into the history of Solomon.
